passages.happening:
“Now when the people saw that Moses was delayed in coming down from the mountain, they gathered around Aaron and said, ‘Come, make us gods who will go before us. As for this Moses who brought us up out of the land of Egypt, we do not know what has happened to him!’” (verse 1).

Aaron tells them to bring their gold earrings (verses 2-3). “He took the gold from their hands, and with an engraving tool he fashioned it into a molten calf. And they said, ‘These, O Israel, are your gods, who brought you up out of the land of Egypt!’” (verse 4).

“When Aaron saw this, he built an altar before the calf and proclaimed: ‘Tomorrow shall be a feast to the LORD’” (verse 5). The next day they offer sacrifices. “And the people sat down to eat and drink, and got up to indulge in revelry” (verse 6).
passages.hearers:
For seven chapters Moses has been on the mountain, receiving plans for a tent where God will live among his people. At the foot of the mountain, after forty days, the people give up waiting. They make a god they can see.

The covenant of chapter 24 is broken within weeks. The people had said twice, ‘we will do’. Now the first two of the Ten Commandments are broken in one act (20:3-4). This is Israel's fall, as Genesis 3 was the fall of the first man and woman.

Why a calf? Bull images were everywhere in Israel's world. In Egypt the Apis bull was honored at Memphis. In texts from Ugarit the high god El is called Bull, and the storm god Baal was linked with a bull's strength. A small silver-plated calf from Canaanite worship was found at Ashkelon in 1990.

The people ask for gods ‘who will go before us’. In the ancient world an image was how a god was made present and carried along. With Moses gone, they want a sign of God's presence they can see, and they want it on their own terms.

Many scholars think the calf was not meant to replace the LORD. It was meant to stand for him, or to be a pedestal on which the unseen God stood, as the cherubim were his throne. Aaron's words support that: ‘a feast to the LORD’. If so, the lesson is sharper. The people used the right name and the right story of rescue, and still broke the covenant. Idolatry is not only worshiping another god. It is also worshiping the true God in a form we make and control.

The gold came from their earrings, much of it the gifts of Egypt (12:35-36). It was the same kind of gift God had just asked for the tabernacle (25:3). What was meant for God's dwelling went into the calf.

‘Indulge in revelry’ translates a word that means to laugh or play. Some interpreters think it hints at sexual play. Others take it as wild feasting. The text does not say more.
passages.later:
Centuries later King Jeroboam set up two golden calves and said almost the same words: “Here, O Israel, are your gods, who brought you up out of the land of Egypt” (1 Kings 12:28).

A psalm remembers the day: “At Horeb they made a calf and worshiped a molten image. They exchanged their Glory for the image of a grass-eating ox” (Psalm 106:19-20).

Paul quotes verse 6 to the church at Corinth as a warning to Christians: “Do not be idolaters, as some of them were” (1 Corinthians 10:7).
passages.hard:
Does this chapter give Christians a reason to look down on the Jewish people?

No. This is Israel's own Scripture, telling the truth about Israel's own sin. A people that keeps a story like this in its holy book is doing something rare and honest. Paul does not use the calf against Israel. He uses it as a warning to the church: ‘These things took place as examples’ (1 Corinthians 10:6). The psalm that remembers the calf is a prayer of confession that says ‘we’.

For centuries some Christians used the New Testament to justify contempt for Jews. That reading is false, and this site rejects it. The note on Acts 2:22-28 sets out why. The right way to read the calf is as a mirror. Every people, and every church, has made gods to its own design.
passages.asks: The people could not bear to wait, so they made a god they could see. Ask what you reach for when God seems slow or silent. And ask whether you ever use God's name for something you have really shaped to suit yourself.

passages.happening:
“Then the LORD said to Moses, ‘Go down at once, for your people, whom you brought up out of the land of Egypt, have corrupted themselves’” (verse 7). “I have seen this people, and they are indeed a stiff-necked people. Now leave Me alone, so that My anger may burn against them and consume them. Then I will make you into a great nation” (verses 9-10).

“But Moses sought the favor of the LORD his God, saying, ‘O LORD, why does Your anger burn against Your people, whom You brought out of the land of Egypt with great power and a mighty hand?’” (verse 11). Why should the Egyptians say he brought them out to kill them (verse 12)? “Remember Your servants Abraham, Isaac, and Israel, to whom You swore by Your very self” (verse 13).

“So the LORD relented from the calamity He had threatened to bring on His people” (verse 14).
passages.hearers:
God tells Moses what has happened below, and he says ‘your people, whom you brought up’. It sounds as if he is disowning them. Moses hands them straight back: ‘Your people, whom You brought out’.

‘Stiff-necked’ is a farmer's picture. An ox that stiffens its neck will not be turned by the yoke.

God offers to begin again with Moses alone, as he once began with Abraham. Moses refuses. He does not excuse the people. He has no good thing to say of them. He gives God two reasons, and both are about God. The first is God's name among the nations: what will Egypt say? The second is God's sworn promise to Abraham, Isaac and Israel. Moses prays God's own words back to him.

And God relents. The Hebrew word, nacham, means to be sorry or to change course. It can also mean to comfort.

Many readers have noticed the words ‘leave Me alone’. God tells Moses what he is about to do, and so leaves a door open for Moses to stand in. The psalm says Moses “stood before Him in the breach to divert His wrath from destroying them” (Psalm 106:23). The Bible presents this prayer as something that mattered.
passages.later:
Moses tells the story again in Deuteronomy: “I fell down before the LORD for forty days and forty nights” (Deuteronomy 9:18), and “the LORD listened to me this time as well” (Deuteronomy 9:19).

The prophets knew this pattern. God says through Jeremiah, “if that nation I warned turns from its evil, then I will relent of the disaster I had planned to bring” (Jeremiah 18:8).

Hebrews says of Christ, “He always lives to intercede for them” (Hebrews 7:25).
passages.hard:
How can God relent, if God does not change?

The Bible says both things. Here ‘the LORD relented’. Elsewhere, “God is not a man, that He should lie, or a son of man, that He should change His mind” (Numbers 23:19).

Christians have read this in two main ways. Classical theology, held by most of the church, teaches that God does not change, and that words like ‘relented’ describe how his settled purpose looks from our side. On this reading God meant all along to spare Israel through Moses' prayer, and invited that prayer with the words ‘leave Me alone’. Others, among them those called open theists, take the words more directly. They hold that God truly responds to prayer and alters his course.

These notes take no side. Both agree on what the chapter teaches: prayer for others matters to God, and Moses' prayer was no empty form.
passages.asks: Moses prayed for people who had nothing to commend them, and he prayed God's own promises back to him. Ask whom you have given up praying for. And ask what promise of God you could hold up to him on their behalf.

passages.happening:
Moses goes down with the two tablets. “The tablets were the work of God, and the writing was the writing of God, engraved on the tablets” (verse 16).

Joshua hears shouting and thinks it is war. Moses says, “I hear the sound of singing!” (verse 18). “As Moses approached the camp and saw the calf and the dancing, he burned with anger and threw the tablets out of his hands, shattering them at the base of the mountain” (verse 19). He burns the calf, grinds it to powder, scatters it on the water and makes the Israelites drink it (verse 20).

“What did this people do to you,” Moses asks Aaron, “that you have led them into so great a sin?” (verse 21). Aaron answers that the people are ‘intent on evil’ (verse 22), and says of the gold, “when I threw it into the fire, out came this calf!” (verse 24).
passages.hearers:
The tablets are described with care just before they are broken: God's work, God's writing. That is what is about to lie in pieces.

Breaking them was more than a burst of temper. In the ancient world, to smash the tablet of a treaty or a contract could mean that the agreement was void. The covenant had been broken in the camp. Moses breaks its written form at the foot of the mountain, in front of the people.

Then the calf is burned, ground and scattered. This was a familiar picture of complete destruction. The god that was to ‘go before’ them ends as dust in their drinking water. The drinking may recall the test in Numbers 5, where a wife suspected of unfaithfulness drinks holy water. The prophets later called idolatry adultery, and the scene fits that picture.

Aaron's answer is almost comic. The narrator has already said that he shaped the calf with a tool. In Aaron's telling he only threw gold into the fire and a calf came out. He blames the people, and then the fire. It is the oldest move in the Bible: the man in the garden blamed the woman, and the woman blamed the serpent.

The Bible does not hide the failure of its leaders. Aaron is the man for whom the holy garments of chapter 28 were designed.
passages.later:
Moses adds something in Deuteronomy that Exodus does not say: “The LORD was angry enough with Aaron to destroy him, but at that time I also prayed for Aaron” (Deuteronomy 9:20).

Stephen retells the story: “At that time they made a calf and offered a sacrifice to the idol, rejoicing in the works of their hands” (Acts 7:41).

The first excuse is in Genesis: “The woman whom You gave me, she gave me fruit from the tree, and I ate” (Genesis 3:12).
passages.asks: Aaron said the calf simply came out of the fire. Ask what you have made, or allowed, and then spoken of as if it just happened. And ask whether you lead people toward what they want, or toward what is right, when the two are not the same.

passages.happening:
“Moses saw that the people were out of control, for Aaron had let them run wild and become a laughingstock to their enemies” (verse 25).

“So Moses stood at the entrance to the camp and said, ‘Whoever is for the LORD, come to me.’ And all the Levites gathered around him” (verse 26).

He tells them that the LORD says each man is to take his sword and go through the camp “from gate to gate, and slay his brother, his friend, and his neighbor” (verse 27). “The Levites did as Moses commanded, and that day about three thousand of the people fell dead” (verse 28).

“Afterward, Moses said, ‘Today you have been ordained for service to the LORD, since each man went against his son and his brother; so the LORD has bestowed a blessing on you this day’” (verse 29).
passages.hearers:
This is the hardest scene in the chapter, and it is told in a few plain lines.

The camp is still in uproar. Moses stands at the gate and calls for a decision: ‘Whoever is for the LORD, come to me’. His own tribe, the Levites, come. They are sent through the camp with swords, and about three thousand die.

The words ‘ordained for service’ are, in Hebrew, the same idiom used for the priests: to fill the hand. The tribe of Levi is set apart for the service of God from this day. It is a costly and sorrowful beginning. The text says they did not spare even those closest to them.

The writer does not linger over the deaths, and neither should a reader. No number is cheered. The next verse begins, ‘The next day’, with Moses going back up the mountain to plead for the people who remain.
passages.later:
Moses' last blessing remembers Levi's choice: “He disregarded his brothers and did not know his own sons, for he kept Your word and maintained Your covenant” (Deuteronomy 33:9).

Jesus placed his own kingdom under a different rule: “My kingdom is not of this world; if it were, My servants would fight” (John 18:36). When Peter drew a sword, Jesus said, “Put your sword back in its place” (Matthew 26:52).
passages.hard:
How can the killing of three thousand people be right?

Many readers find these verses deeply troubling, and that response should not be brushed aside. These notes do not make the scene smaller than it is. Three thousand people died by the sword, at the hands of their own kin, on the word Moses gave as the LORD's.

Several things can be said about what the text itself presents. It frames the killing as the judgment of the covenant, in a camp where God himself was king, on a people who had sworn to that covenant only weeks before. It falls on a rebellion that was still running wild. And Moses first gives a call, ‘Whoever is for the LORD, come to me’, which suggests that those who died were those who held to the calf. The nation is not destroyed. Some critical scholars read the story mainly as an account of how the Levites came to their sacred office.

None of that removes the weight, and it should not. Some thoughtful Christians say plainly that this is a place where they must trust what they cannot fully see.

One thing is certain. This is not a pattern. Christians generally hold that it belonged to Israel as a nation under God's direct rule, at one moment in its story. The church was never given a sword. Jesus put his kingdom under his word, and the apostles' discipline goes no further than putting a person out of the fellowship, in hope of winning him back (1 Corinthians 5). No one may use these verses to justify violence in God's name against any person or people, in a family, a church or a nation. When Christians have done so, they have sinned against the Lord they claimed to serve.
passages.asks: Moses asked who was for the LORD, and the answer cost the Levites dearly. Ask what loyalty to God has cost you, and whether there is a loyalty you have put above him. Then remember that Jesus told his follower to put his sword away, and ask whether your zeal for God ever turns into harshness toward people.

passages.happening:
“The next day Moses said to the people, ‘You have committed a great sin. Now I will go up to the LORD; perhaps I can make atonement for your sin’” (verse 30).

He prays, “Oh, what a great sin these people have committed! They have made gods of gold for themselves. Yet now, if You would only forgive their sin.... But if not, please blot me out of the book that You have written” (verses 31-32).

“The LORD replied to Moses, ‘Whoever has sinned against Me, I will blot out of My book. Now go, lead the people to the place I described. Behold, My angel shall go before you. But on the day I settle accounts, I will punish them for their sin’” (verses 33-34). And a plague comes on the people (verse 35).
passages.hearers:
Moses goes up again. This time he has seen the sin with his own eyes, and he does not soften it. Three times the chapter calls it ‘a great sin’ (verses 21, 30 and 31).

His prayer breaks off in the middle. ‘If You would only forgive their sin’, and the sentence is never finished. Then he offers himself. If the people cannot be forgiven, let his own name be wiped from God's book. The word for ‘blot out’ is used of wiping a dish clean or rubbing out writing. The book is the record of the living who belong to God.

It is one of the great moments of love in the Old Testament. The man who was offered a new nation of his own asks to be lost with the old one.

God declines the offer. Each person answers for his own sin. Moses cannot make atonement by giving up himself. But God does not end the story either. Moses is to lead the people on, and an angel will go before them. The judgment is real and it is held back. The people live, the promise to Abraham stands, and the chapter ends with the question still open: will God himself go with a people like this? The next chapter takes it up.
passages.later:
Paul felt what Moses felt for the same people: “For I could wish that I myself were cursed and cut off from Christ for the sake of my brothers, my own flesh and blood” (Romans 9:3).

The book comes back in the Bible's last pages. The risen Christ promises the one who overcomes, “I will never blot out his name from the Book of Life” (Revelation 3:5).

The New Testament says that Jesus did what Moses offered and could not do. Paul writes, “Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us” (Galatians 3:13).
passages.asks: Moses asked to be blotted out if his people could not be forgiven. Ask whether you love anyone enough to pray like that. And ask what it means to you that the New Testament says Christ bore the curse so that your name would stay in the book.
